pass_a_gloss: What is the reason for the silence of the many, and especially now, and for my being forced to be silent, both willingly and unwillingly, and to be compelled to keep silent? I have indeed neglected the beautiful and elegant words, which are spoken or written in order by the chosen and approved names and verbs, without any hindrance. For an eight-year span is already mine, since when I have not spoken or written anything, either privately or publicly, except for the wonderful men who have cultivated beautiful philosophy, to whom elegance and refinement of names are of little concern. But setting their voices in the second rank, they wish to investigate and proclaim the matters themselves with precision. Perhaps they are not unwilling, but rather very willing to pour out the beautiful and precise thoughts in a careless and unpolished way, but maybe they are unable to do so, having the sacred and divine power and the eloquent word in their souls, which is difficult to contain. If indeed silence is a friend and helper to the mind and discovery, the eloquent word is not found elsewhere, but in the voices and continuous practice. But the mind is also seized by another kind of learning, and the mouth is bound by the tongue, if I wanted to say something, even small, to the Greek voice, our wonderful men, who now direct the affairs of all men under the human rule, not being careless or ignorant. Being themselves accurate and varied and wonderful, and being called totally Greek, expressed and handed down in the Roman voice, which is impressive and boastful and conforming to the royal authority, but burdensome to me. Since, however, our words are like images of the passions of our soul, to those who are able to speak, like good painters, with technique and with the material of colors, not only similar but also varied and beautiful, to write the writings without any hindrance, we would agree.

pass_b_english: What is the reason for the silence of the many, and especially for me now, both willingly and unwillingly being muzzled and compelled to keep silent? For I have indeed neglected these beautiful and elegant words, which are spoken or composed without hindrance in unbroken sequence by chosen and approved names and verbs. For an eight-year span is already mine, since which time I have not happened to speak or write anything at all, either great or small, nor have I heard anyone else writing or speaking privately, or providing public panegyric and contest speeches, except those wonderful men who have cultivated beautiful philosophy; to them elegance and refinement of names are of little concern, but setting their voices in second place, they wish to investigate and proclaim the matters themselves with precision. They are not unwilling, I think, but rather very willing to pour out the beautiful and precise thoughts in a careless and unadorned way through speech; but perhaps they are unable to do so, having the sacred and God-given power in their thoughts and the eloquent word in their expressions, two things that are most opposite, for each of two men to grasp the greater share in one and the same — and that a small and human — soul. If indeed silence is a friend and helper in some way to the mind and discovery, the eloquent word is not found elsewhere by seeking, but in voices and their continuous practice.

But the mind is also seized by another kind of learning, and the mouth binds the tongue, if I should wish to say anything, even something small, in the Greek voice. Our wonderful men, who now direct the affairs of all men under human rule, are neither careless nor learning ignorantly; being themselves accurate, varied, and wonderful, and to sum up, totally Greek in expression; yet expressed and handed over to the Roman voice, which is awe-inspiring and boastful and conforming to the royal authority, but burdensome to me. Nor would it have been possible or desirable for me to be otherwise at any time. Since, however, our words are nothing other than images of the passions of our soul, to those able to speak — like good painters, with technique most technical, and rich in the material of colors — we would agree that they can write the writings without any hindrance, not only likenesses but also varied and very beautiful ones, with the intermingling of the flowers.
notes: The translation aims to preserve the original Greek text's meaning and structure, including the complex argument about the difficulty of containing the sacred/divine power and the eloquent word within a single human soul.

review.notes: Pass A fails on completeness and accuracy regarding the 'two men' / 'soul' clause. The Greek text 'δύο ἀνθρώπων ἰδίᾳ ἕχάστου {πλεονγδεχτήματα, μιᾷ καὶ τῇ αὐτῇ, καὶ ταύτῃ μιχρᾷ καὶ ἀνϑρωτείνῃ περιλαβεῖν ψυχῆ, ὄντα τως ζἐναντλιώτατα' describes the difficulty of one soul grasping two things that belong to two men (or are as if belonging to two men) because they are most opposite. Pass A omits the entire complex clause regarding the 'two men' and the 'soul' being 'most opposite' (ὄντα τως ζἐναντλιώτατα), providing only a vague summary: 'which is difficult to contain.' Pass B is more complete but Pass A is a required component of the check. Additionally, Pass A omits the final clause 'κατὰ μηδὲν ἐμσοδιζομένοις' (not encroaching upon anything/without hindrance) and the specific imagery of 'the intermingling of the flowers' (πολυμιγεῖ τῶν ἀνθῶν) which is present in the Greek but missing in Pass A.
reasons: Pass A omits the significant clause 'δύο ἀνθρώπων ἰδίᾳ ἕχάστου... ὄντα τως ζἐναντλιώτατα' (which Pass A reduces to 'which is difficult to contain') and the final imagery 'πολυμιγεῖ τῶν ἀνθῶν' (the intermingling of the flowers).
Pass A omits the phrase 'κατὰ μηδὲν ἐμσοδιζομένοις' (not encroaching upon anything/without hindrance) in the final sentence.
